results.title: "Perfectly-Integrated" African Migrant On Trial For Strangling, Dismembering His Wife
results.description: "Perfectly-Integrated" African Migrant On Trial For Strangling, Dismembering His Wife Via Remix News An African man, who was described as "perfectly integrated," is on trial in Bonn on charges connected to the strangling murder of his wife, whom he then dismembered. The woman's remains were later found in several locations across Germany, according to court proceedings. Asmerom G., 42, an Eritrean national, faces the charges in Bonn Regional Court in North Rhine-Westphalia. The case stems from events in mid-November 2025 involving his wife, Weghata A., 32. The couple had married in Ethiopia in 2019, and she arrived in Germany in 2024 through family reunification. The defendant allegedly met his wife, 32-year-old Weghata A., inside his car, where they began arguing on their way back from a church visit. According to Bonner Generalanzeiger newspaper, Asmerom G. later told police that his wife told him their 3-month-old girl was not his biological child. He reportedly could not remember what happened next. According to prosecutors, Asmerom G. then strangled his wife in the back seat of the car in a parking lot in Bonn, directly in front of the baby who was sitting in a child seat. After the crime, the defendant is said to have driven with the body and the baby in the car to the Monastery of Saint Anthony, 160 kilometers away, where he abandoned the little girl in the stroller when it was only 2 degrees Celsius (35 degrees Fahrenheit). Fortunately for the girl, monks found the child just 40 minutes after she was dropped off. Asmerom G. then went to work dismembering Weghata's body, including packing her hands and head in plastic bags. He left the torso behind, which was found at the end of November 2025. Asmerom G. left the body parts on the side of the autobahn, on the A45. The head of the woman was discovered by garbage collectors in April 2026. Asmerom G. was arrested in Ethiopia and extradited to Germany. He has a prior conviction for aggravated assault. On the first day of the trial, he declined to comment on the allegations. Defense attorney Martin Kretschmer has said the case rests largely on DNA evidence and mobile-phone data. Kretschmer told Bild newspaper, "Until his arrest, he was considered perfectly integrated." German media was even singing his praises in 2016. The man from Eritrea had landed a job as an electrical assistant at a firm in Rheinbach, in North Rhine-Westphalia, and gave interviews about leaving his homeland three years earlier to escape political persecution. He wanted German citizenship, he said. His boss at the time was quick to describe Asmerom G. as talented, reliable, and "capable of anything," according to Bild newspaper. However, then trouble began. Within a year, Asmerom G. was in trouble with the law. A brawl led to a conviction for grievous bodily harm at Siegburg District Court, earning him a six-month suspended sentence. He moved on from Rheinbach and took up work behind the wheel of a freight truck. Somewhere along the way, he made a trip back to his home country - for reasons that remain unclear - and returned to Germany with a woman named Weghata A., who was 31 at the time, his wife under Eritrean law. On July 26, 2025, she delivered their daughter. The child is now in the care of authorities. Lawyer Gesine Ickert, representing the daughter and the deceased's father, has stated that the child is well looked after under the circumstances. The trial continues. Tyler Durden Fri, 10/16/2026 - 06:30

results.title: China defends trade surplus, blames export controls
results.description: Chinese Premier Li Qian this week pushed back against criticism of his country’s burgeoning trade surplus by blaming export controls that countries have imposed on China and other factors outside of Beijing’s control. Analysts, meanwhile, contend that China and its trading partners need to reframe the issue of Chinese overcapacity for any amenable solution to be possible. China is on track to set a new record for its trade surplus with other countries, according to data issued Wednesday by its General Administration of Customs. Its surplus through September was $938.1 billion, with exports up 16.4 percent year-over-year to about $3.47 trillion and imports up 22.3 percent to about $2.5 trillion. “It is unrealistic to expect trade balance while simultaneously imposing export controls; this will only drive up costs, disrupt supply chains, and further exacerbate imbalances,” Li said during a speech at China’s Import and Export Fair, according to an informal translation. “What we need is an ‘upward balance’ of expanding openness and jointly growing the ‘pie,’ not a ‘downward balance’ of closing markets and inevitably leading to shrinkage.” The U.S. in recent years has imposed a series of export controls on sensitive technology products, cutting off Chinese access. Li touted China’s import volume, which he said has been second globally for 17 straight years. “At the same time, China's high-quality exports, especially innovative products, are continuously driving new growth in the global market,” he added. “China is willing to work with all countries to continue building an open world economy, strengthen connectivity and integration, expand the global market, and bring greater benefits to all parties.” The Chinese premier also sought to refute rhetoric often used by U.S. officials, particularly President Trump, who say China’s trade surplus means it is taking advantage of the U.S. “We must recognize that the essence of trade is mutual benefit; we cannot simply assume that a trade surplus means ‘taking advantage’ or a trade deficit means ‘losing out,’” Li said. “Trade balance naturally approaches through mutually beneficial interactions where all parties obtain what they need, not through building walls or even suppression.” “When discussing China's trade, some people often only see the import and export figures, failing to consider the underlying real effects,” he continued. “China is both a ‘super seller’ and a ‘super buyer.’ As a ‘super seller,’ we bring more of a ‘neighborly benefit effect’ to all parties.” “China never deliberately pursues a trade surplus,” Li added, claiming that any surplus is also a benefit to its trading partners. Chinese overcapacity, long believed to be a contributing factor to Beijing’s persistent trade surpluses, can be a benefit to trading partners if limited to certain industries, according to Nicholas Lamp, an associate professor at Queen’s University international law program. “The truth is that in many sectors we are benefitting from Chinese oversupply -- it results in cheap products for us,” he said on the Peterson Institute for International Economics’ Trade Winds podcast Wednesday. “Not just in terms of affordability, but in terms of sustainability. We have to keep in mind that our really only hope to tackle climate change is on the basis of Chinese production of solar panels and batteries.” Trading partners should “develop a differentiated approach to trade with China in different sectors and different products,” Lamp continued, discerning between sectors with national security concerns and those without. Lamp pointed to U.S.-China Board of Trade established after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington, DC, last month. The board is a government-to-government mechanism to lower tariffs on non-strategic goods. “I think it gets at the basic message that not all trade has to be politicized,” he said. “Not all trade is problematic in the same way.” “And so I think this is something that’s really important here, that we look at specific sectors and really ask ourselves is this something where we can be happy to be completely dependent on China?” he added. The answer for toys and consumer electronics, Lamp contended, is yes. China and its partners need to reframe the trade debate around China, said Yeling Tan, a Peterson senior fellow, during the podcast. “There’s, in a sense, a very narrow corridor that all sides need to find their way toward,” she said. “For China, it is a kind of reassurance that, no the world or the western world is not out to contain China. It is not out to suppress China or to encircle China.” China also must work to reassure its partners by addressing their trade concerns. “What we’re seeing from China is sort of a proliferation of the security framing across so many parts of its economy and society,” Tan said. “I think China needs to put more weight into recognizing that some of the structural imbalances does create pain for its trading partners and that pain is a problem for China, it’s not just a problem for the trading partner itself to solve.” The trade data published by Beijing this week, however, shows that it is not looking to address those concerns, Bruegel senior fellow Alicia García-Herrero said. China’s export growth is accelerating, she said on the podcast, which means its trade surplus is growing. “There’s no self-correction. It’s the opposite,” she said. “Unless something happens, this will not self-correct.” -- Brett Fortnam (bfortnam@iwpnews.com)

results.title: Agriculture Ministry Aims to Promote Quality Food and Wine to Attract Tourists
results.description: Bulgaria aims to produce high-quality food that can be promoted to attract tourists, Agriculture Minister Plamen Abrovski said at a tourism conference in Plovdiv on Friday. He highlighted the country’s distinctive products, including dairy products, traditional Bulgarian yoghurt and local wines. Abrovski also noted his long-standing connection to the wine industry, having begun his professional career at Bulgaria’s Executive Agency on Vine and Wine in 2004. He emphasized that his current role as minister allows him to oversee food production, quality and safety. The forum took place at the University of Food Technologies (UFT) in Plovdiv, organized jointly with the National Tourism Board in partnership with the Tourism Ministry.
